title: Raising the dead
subtitle: De-extinction promises to reverse some of humanity's worst ecological mistakes. We should be clear about what it can and cannot do.

paragraphs.text: In 2003, in a Spanish laboratory, a goat was born that belonged to a species which had officially ceased to exist three years earlier. The animal was a clone of the last Pyrenean ibex, or bucardo, whose cells had been frozen before she died in 2000. The kid survived for only a few minutes, killed by a lung defect, and the bucardo thus earned the melancholy distinction of being the first species to become extinct twice. Yet the experiment demonstrated, however fleetingly, that extinction need not be absolutely final – and since then the ambition has grown from a scientific curiosity into a lavishly funded enterprise.

It is worth being precise about what 'de-extinction' actually involves, because the word promises rather more than any of its techniques can deliver. Cloning, the method used for the bucardo, requires living cells or at least well-preserved nuclei, which rules it out for almost every lost species. The mammoth, despite the well-preserved carcasses found in Siberia, has left behind only fragmented DNA. What is proposed instead is to edit the genome of its closest living relative, the Asian elephant, inserting variants associated with dense hair, thick layers of fat and blood that functions at low temperatures. The result would not be a mammoth but a cold-tolerant elephant: a proxy engineered to resemble, and perhaps behave like, the original.

A similar logic underlies efforts to revive the passenger pigeon, a bird whose flocks, numbering in the billions, once darkened North American skies for hours. Relentless commercial hunting and the clearance of eastern forests drove it to extinction with astonishing speed; the last known individual, a female named Martha, died at Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. Here the plan is to modify the genome of a close relative, the band-tailed pigeon. The difficulty is not merely genetic. Passenger pigeons appear to have depended on vast numbers for feeding, breeding and protection from predators, and nobody knows whether a few hundred engineered birds could ever learn to live as the species once did.

The oldest approach of all requires no genetic engineering whatsoever. The aurochs, the immense wild ox from which domestic cattle descend, died out in 1627 when the last cow perished in a Polish forest. Because fragments of its genetic inheritance survive, scattered across modern breeds, it is in principle possible to reassemble something like the original through selective breeding. The first attempt, by two German zoo directors in the 1920s and 1930s, produced the so-called Heck cattle, which were smaller than the aurochs and resembled it only superficially. More recent European programmes are better informed, using the sequenced genome of the aurochs to choose which hardy, primitive breeds to cross, and their animals already graze in several rewilding areas. Here the goal is avowedly ecological rather than sentimental: large grazers that prevent open landscapes from becoming overgrown.

Advocates advance three principal arguments. The first is ecological: restored species could fill roles that have stood vacant since their disappearance. Some suggest that herds of mammoth-like animals might help to maintain the Arctic tundra as grassland and, by trampling snow, slow the thawing of carbon-rich permafrost. The second is technological: the same genetic tools might help rescue endangered species that survive in perilously small numbers. The third is more emotional, though no less real: the prospect of seeing a mammoth, or something like one, has generated public enthusiasm and private investment on a scale that more conventional conservation projects rarely achieve.

Each of these claims deserves scrutiny. The permafrost argument rests on calculations that would require hundreds of thousands of animals – a population that would take centuries to build up from elephants that carry a single calf for almost two years. Moreover, those surrogate mothers would themselves belong to an endangered species, raising serious questions about animal welfare. The danger I find most compelling, however, is subtler. If extinction comes to be seen as reversible, the urgency of protecting threatened habitats may weaken. Economists call this 'moral hazard': people who believe they are insured against a loss tend to take fewer precautions against it. There is also the matter of money. Every pound spent on resurrecting the dead is potentially a pound not spent on the living, and one study estimated that maintaining revived species could result in a net loss of biodiversity if it diverted resources from existing programmes.

Nor does the way such projects are publicised help. In 2025 one company announced the birth of three white-coated wolf pups that it described as revived dire wolves, a species that vanished more than ten thousand years ago. Specialists quickly pointed out that the animals were grey wolves carrying a small number of edited genes. Announcements of this kind risk persuading the public that the scientific problems have been solved when they have barely been defined.

None of this means that the research should be abandoned. The techniques it is producing, from better methods of reading ancient DNA to editing genes for disease resistance, may well prove valuable to conservation in other ways. But we should be honest about what is being created. The animals that emerge will be new organisms, shaped by present-day preferences and released into ecosystems that have changed profoundly since their predecessors disappeared. De-extinction, properly understood, is not a means of undoing the past; it is one more way in which humans decide what the future natural world will contain. Whether we decide wisely will depend less on the brilliance of the science than on the honesty of the debate surrounding it.

items.statement: The cloning of the bucardo showed that an extinct species could be restored on a lasting basis.
items.evidence: The kid survived for only a few minutes
items.note: The writer says the experiment worked only 'fleetingly' - the clone died within minutes, so the restoration was anything but lasting.

items.statement: The term 'de-extinction' gives an exaggerated impression of what is scientifically possible.
items.evidence: the word promises rather more than any of its techniques can deliver

items.statement: Cloning cannot be used to revive the great majority of extinct animals.
items.evidence: which rules it out for almost every lost species

items.statement: More well-preserved mammoth remains have been found in Siberia than anywhere else.
items.note: The writer mentions well-preserved carcasses found in Siberia, but makes no comparison with mammoth remains found in any other region.

items.statement: Hunting played a greater part than the loss of forests in the extinction of the passenger pigeon.
items.note: Both hunting and forest clearance are named as causes, but the writer never says which was more important.

items.statement: The cattle produced by the first back-breeding attempt looked very similar to the aurochs.
items.note: Heck cattle were also smaller than the aurochs; any likeness was only on the surface.

items.stem: According to the writer, what is a particular obstacle to reviving the passenger pigeon?
options: The band-tailed pigeon is too distantly related to provide a suitable genome.
The bird's survival may have relied on living in extremely large groups.
The forests where the bird once lived have entirely disappeared.
Revived birds might once again be hunted for commercial purposes.
items.evidence: Passenger pigeons appear to have depended on vast numbers for feeding, breeding and protection from predators
items.note: C and D recycle the passage's causes of extinction (forest clearance, commercial hunting), but the writer presents neither as an obstacle to revival; A contradicts 'a close relative'.

items.stem: How do recent European aurochs programmes differ from the first attempt?
options: They alter the genes of domestic cattle directly.
They are aimed at producing animals for zoos.
They have produced animals larger than the original aurochs.
They are guided by knowledge of the aurochs' DNA.
items.evidence: using the sequenced genome of the aurochs to choose which hardy, primitive breeds to cross
items.note: A is wrong because back-breeding 'requires no genetic engineering whatsoever'; B confuses the zoo directors of the first attempt with the aims of the new programmes.

items.stem: The writer mentions the trampling of snow as an example of how revived animals might
options: help to reduce a process linked to climate change.
damage the vegetation of the Arctic tundra.
find it difficult to survive in the far north.
items.evidence: by trampling snow, slow the thawing of carbon-rich permafrost

items.stem: What is the writer's main criticism of the announcement about dire wolves?
options: It exaggerated the length of time since the species had disappeared.
It ignored the welfare of the animals involved.
It could mislead people about how much progress has been made.
It relied on genetic techniques that specialists considered unsafe.
items.evidence: Announcements of this kind risk persuading the public that the scientific problems have been solved when they have barely been defined.
items.note: D borrows 'specialists' and 'genes' from the paragraph, but the specialists objected that the pups were not dire wolves, not that the methods were unsafe.

groups.title: Objections to de-extinction
lines: The writer doubts that revived mammoths could protect the permafrost, as this would require an enormous {1} of animals, which could only be achieved very slowly. Using elephants as surrogate mothers also raises concerns about the {2} of the animals involved. More seriously, if people believe that extinction can be undone, they may become less committed to protecting endangered {3}. Finally, spending on de-extinction could reduce the {4} available for existing conservation work.

answers.evidence: would require hundreds of thousands of animals
answers.note: D (variety) fits the grammar but the problem described is sheer numbers, not diversity.

answers.evidence: raising serious questions about animal welfare
answers.note: I (fertility) is tempting because of the long pregnancy, but the concern the writer names is welfare.

answers.evidence: the urgency of protecting threatened habitats may weaken
if it diverted resources from existing programmes
